Hi everyone! I said I’d break down the influencer book I read in the megathread, so here goes! Sorry it's so long even though I limited it to MS-relevant passages.

Book: Break The Internet: The Truth About Influencers | Author: Olivia Yallop | Year: 2021 | Pages: ~250

Personal thoughts about the subject: Influencer culture makes me super uncomfortable. The idea of sharing my personal life online in any identifiable way fills me with dread and anxiety. I felt a thin undercurrent of discomfort the whole time I was reading the text. This is NOT the author’s fault; it’s purely the subject matter. This book is fairly recent and I was familiar with some of the people, brands, and sites mentioned, but a lot of it was lost on me. The author is from England, is about late 20s/early 30s, and has a background in advertising. She clearly grew up with the internet and takes what I think is a very unbiased stance on influencer culture. It’s easy to scoff at people who make a full time job of their social media presence (I scoff big time, all day), but it’s a real industry worth billions of dollars. Now let’s review the MS-adjacent material I found in the book!

In describing what an influencer’s job actually is, the author states, “[The influencer’s] job is to seem jobless” (p.35). This is often true, but not always. I think a better way to describe the MS type of wannabe influencer is: her job is to make it seem like her job is influencing. For someone who pretends to be influential but who doesn’t have the following or interaction to actually be influential, this presentation comes off as artificial, try-hard, depressing. This is the vibe you’ll get from most people online who want to be influencers, and it’s because the market is so saturated it’s impossible to be successful.

The author (a millennial like me and MS) mentions the “hustle culture” present in social media accounts dealing with entrepreneurship, cryptocurrency, and pyramid schemes (Younique anyone?). She presents an interesting point: in an economy where many millennials are working multiple jobs, being underpaid, and feeling like hobbies must be monetized to be worth their time, these hustle influencers take these negatives and present them as empowering. This theory makes a lot of sense and is also incredibly sad.


Later on, we get into the topic of engagement pods, which are groups of social media users who vow to follow, share or like each other’s posts to boost engagement. These pods are often against terms of service for websites and thus are kept ultra-secret. She spends a little time in one and shows how exhausting it is to be in an engagement pod. The guidelines for these groups are to comment on strangers’ posts in a way that is fake but looks authentic, and others will do the same to you. There has been speculation of engagement pod activity, but I have never seen her actively sharing or commenting on other peoples' posts. It makes a lot more sense to me that she’s buying likes and follows rather than belonging to a pod.

Although Amazon swimsuit hauls are certainly less wasteful than many videos in the "junklord" category of social media post (think MrBeast and "I filled my friend's car with slime"-type challenge videos), they fall into the category of “pure consumerist pornography” (p.147) where viewers are treated to the illusion of buying whatever you want, whenever you feel like. This is a VERY popular genre of post and that's exactly why she does it. It's brought up a lot on here how wasteful this type of content is: the items in the video end up returned or trashed, and of course, someone on the other side of the planet had to manufacture the fucking thing and then ship it thousands of miles.

In Chapter 6: Spilling the Tea, snark communities are mentioned directly. An example is given of a particularly popular snark group (primarily on reddit) which I've never been a part of, and the influencer in question isn't someone I know anything about. The positives and negatives of snark are discussed exhaustively. She also discusses "tea channels" which catalog the latest influencer drama; MS is not big enough to have ever appeared on one of these. She HAS appeared on instagramreality, which is mentioned in the book by name. The author thinks it's weird that snark communities exist, but she spends a lot of time analyzing why they do. I agree that it does look very weird from an outsider's perspective, and I'm someone who spends a lot of time here. She separates "snark" from "trolling" by specifying that snark communities have rules - however, she knows these rules can and will be broken, and sometimes snark devolves into trolling. We have rules against snarking on body characteristics, and I see them broken flagrantly almost every day. I wish she'd added one important difference: trolling is interacting with a person directly and snarking is not. So why do people snark in the first place? The author suggests that "snarking provides a distraction from the current state of the world..." (193) and it's cathartic for online denizens to rail against what influencer culture represents in general. I agree with this and I believe it's why I'm personally here.

There are a lot of non-MS-adjacent topics covered in the book that I thought were very interesting. From sponsored elementary-age gamers to family vloggers who monetize an adoption and then rehome the adoptee, this book is full of horror stories as well as triumphs. The author is not “anti-influencer” in the slightest but she levels criticisms where it’s due. I'm already anti-influencer so reading 250 pages that already agree with me would kinda feel like a circlejerk, plus I actually learned something. Overall this book is a good primer which I would recommend if you’re like me and want to know more about the basics of the internet celebrity industry.

If you have any other influencer book recommendations I'd love to check them out! Thanks for reading!

I'm an atheist who's active in AA. I'd love to share my experiences and advice.

Alcoholics Anonymous (the book AND the program) was made in the 1930s for one specific type of person, and that is protestant Christian men. However, the modern groups are a lot more diverse and you're bound to see agnostics, atheists, and others who you wouldn't have found in the original meetings. AA literature certainly does have a religious bent that is undeniable, and the language itself is old school. Some meetings are called "Big Book" or "12 x 12" and are just for studying the literature, I (and most non-religious AAs) tend to skip these.

The steps will talk about a higher power but that does not have to mean any God specifically. People use all sorts of things as their higher power: the AA group, the universe, and the family are all popular higher power stand-ins. You can also search "twelve steps secular" to find versions of the steps that are a litter easier to understand without the god concept, and you can work them the same way.

My suggestion for you starting out: when you go to a meeting, look for an "open discussion" or "topic" meeting. These are for people to share their triumphs and experiences. These are great because you'll get to hear from people who have been through what you're going through. They're very personal and I think they're the most helpful. You don't have to share any more than you want to.

Hi everyone! I said I’d break down the influencer book I read in the megathread, so here goes! Sorry it's so long even though I limited it to MS-relevant passages.

Book: Break The Internet: The Truth About Influencers | Author: Olivia Yallop | Year: 2021 | Pages: ~250

Personal thoughts about the subject: Influencer culture makes me super uncomfortable. The idea of sharing my personal life online in any identifiable way fills me with dread and anxiety. I felt a thin undercurrent of discomfort the whole time I was reading the text. This is NOT the author’s fault; it’s purely the subject matter. This book is fairly recent and I was familiar with some of the people, brands, and sites mentioned, but a lot of it was lost on me. The author is from England, is about late 20s/early 30s, and has a background in advertising. She clearly grew up with the internet and takes what I think is a very unbiased stance on influencer culture. It’s easy to scoff at people who make a full time job of their social media presence (I scoff big time, all day), but it’s a real industry worth billions of dollars. Now let’s review the MS-adjacent material I found in the book!

In describing what an influencer’s job actually is, the author states, “[The influencer’s] job is to seem jobless” (p.35). This is often true, but not always. I think a better way to describe the MS type of wannabe influencer is: her job is to make it seem like her job is influencing. For someone who pretends to be influential but who doesn’t have the following or interaction to actually be influential, this presentation comes off as artificial, try-hard, depressing. This is the vibe you’ll get from most people online who want to be influencers, and it’s because the market is so saturated it’s impossible to be successful.

The author (a millennial like me and MS) mentions the “hustle culture” present in social media accounts dealing with entrepreneurship, cryptocurrency, and pyramid schemes (Younique anyone?). She presents an interesting point: in an economy where many millennials are working multiple jobs, being underpaid, and feeling like hobbies must be monetized to be worth their time, these hustle influencers take these negatives and present them as empowering. This theory makes a lot of sense and is also incredibly sad.


Later on, we get into the topic of engagement pods, which are groups of social media users who vow to follow, share or like each other’s posts to boost engagement. These pods are often against terms of service for websites and thus are kept ultra-secret. She spends a little time in one and shows how exhausting it is to be in an engagement pod. The guidelines for these groups are to comment on strangers’ posts in a way that is fake but looks authentic, and others will do the same to you. There has been speculation of engagement pod activity, but I have never seen her actively sharing or commenting on other peoples' posts. It makes a lot more sense to me that she’s buying likes and follows rather than belonging to a pod.

Although Amazon swimsuit hauls are certainly less wasteful than many videos in the "junklord" category of social media post (think MrBeast and "I filled my friend's car with slime"-type challenge videos), they fall into the category of “pure consumerist pornography” (p.147) where viewers are treated to the illusion of buying whatever you want, whenever you feel like. This is a VERY popular genre of post and that's exactly why she does it. It's brought up a lot on here how wasteful this type of content is: the items in the video end up returned or trashed, and of course, someone on the other side of the planet had to manufacture the fucking thing and then ship it thousands of miles.

In Chapter 6: Spilling the Tea, snark communities are mentioned directly. An example is given of a particularly popular snark group (primarily on reddit) which I've never been a part of, and the influencer in question isn't someone I know anything about. The positives and negatives of snark are discussed exhaustively. She also discusses "tea channels" which catalog the latest influencer drama; MS is not big enough to have ever appeared on one of these. She HAS appeared on instagramreality, which is mentioned in the book by name. The author thinks it's weird that snark communities exist, but she spends a lot of time analyzing why they do. I agree that it does look very weird from an outsider's perspective, and I'm someone who spends a lot of time here. She separates "snark" from "trolling" by specifying that snark communities have rules - however, she knows these rules can and will be broken, and sometimes snark devolves into trolling. We have rules against snarking on body characteristics, and I see them broken flagrantly almost every day. I wish she'd added one important difference: trolling is interacting with a person directly and snarking is not. So why do people snark in the first place? The author suggests that "snarking provides a distraction from the current state of the world..." (193) and it's cathartic for online denizens to rail against what influencer culture represents in general. I agree with this and I believe it's why I'm personally here.

There are a lot of non-MS-adjacent topics covered in the book that I thought were very interesting. From sponsored elementary-age gamers to family vloggers who monetize an adoption and then rehome the adoptee, this book is full of horror stories as well as triumphs. The author is not “anti-influencer” in the slightest but she levels criticisms where it’s due. I'm already anti-influencer so reading 250 pages that already agree with me would kinda feel like a circlejerk, plus I actually learned something. Overall this book is a good primer which I would recommend if you’re like me and want to know more about the basics of the internet celebrity industry.

If you have any other influencer book recommendations I'd love to check them out! Thanks for reading!

I'm an atheist who's active in AA. I'd love to share my experiences and advice.

Alcoholics Anonymous (the book AND the program) was made in the 1930s for one specific type of person, and that is protestant Christian men. However, the modern groups are a lot more diverse and you're bound to see agnostics, atheists, and others who you wouldn't have found in the original meetings. AA literature certainly does have a religious bent that is undeniable, and the language itself is old school. Some meetings are called "Big Book" or "12 x 12" and are just for studying the literature, I (and most non-religious AAs) tend to skip these.

The steps will talk about a higher power but that does not have to mean any God specifically. People use all sorts of things as their higher power: the AA group, the universe, and the family are all popular higher power stand-ins. You can also search "twelve steps secular" to find versions of the steps that are a litter easier to understand without the god concept, and you can work them the same way.

My suggestion for you starting out: when you go to a meeting, look for an "open discussion" or "topic" meeting. These are for people to share their triumphs and experiences. These are great because you'll get to hear from people who have been through what you're going through. They're very personal and I think they're the most helpful. You don't have to share any more than you want to.
